title: Zutty's beat and the grind of Bourbon Street
summary: Watkins explains Zutty's relaxed fast beat, then describes dead nights, long hours, short breaks and police rules at Bourbon Street clubs.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, but I wasn't going there at that time when he was there. But I used to watch him on different advertisements. You know, he used to play on the truck, you know. And I used to listen to his beat all the time. I said, I don't see how that man don't get tired beating like that. Until George told me, he said, that's how Zutty used to beat. This is the way I'm showing you. He said, you can get a faster beat and you won't feel half as tired as if you get it played from the ankle. And he wasn't telling no lie because I never felt tired when I knocked off. I don't care how hard we worked or how long of hours we worked. The only job that killed me was out there on Bourbon Street. On them dead nights bill, I was just as dead as the nights were. Because when you don't have nobody around, you know, to sit down and applaud or ask you for different numbers or something like that or smile up at you, it just kills your spirit. But like on concert, we play at different concerts, man, we get all them applaud shots. I'm ready to kill myself then. See, because I know the people that's enjoying it and they're making me feel good to see they enjoying it. But you catch a dead house, you just don't have no spirit to play nothing. Not even a piano or clarinet or anything. But when the people start to give you applause and hoorah and all like that, well, you're ready to give them a nice work. You ain't gonna worry about the hours passing in. But you sit out there on Bourbon Street up on them bandstand and catch dead nights. You wanna know every time you could be looking at that clock to see what time it is. And that's where I used to be out there and we was working out there. And then with some tough hours, six hours a night. Yeah. It's really hard hours. If you had somewhere to go for them and your break is so short, you don't have time to go nowhere to get, you know, to sit down and just the band sitting back there talking. Well, you wanna be somewhere where you can sit down and talk with different people, you know, or something like that. But we didn't have no chance to do anything like that out there because they brought us out on the sidewalk when we was playing at the Amaraka. They wouldn't let us come out there. We used to go out there on intermission to catch a little fresh air. The police told the provider to keep us off of the sidewalk. But we wasn't working nobody but ourselves.

You know, I've heard that they did that too. Yeah. Still, I have seen a couple of musicians sometimes would go up and hear another band outside like Paul Barber and you're playing. Yeah, you could do that, yeah. Or somebody would go up and hear another band.
Because when we was working at Mardi Gras, Bill and them used to come down and listen to us and we used to go down and listen to them, you know.
Yeah, when Paul was out there we used to go over there and listen to him too, you know, and they'd come by us and listen.
It's hard to have time and 15 minutes to get there.

If you don't have no time, no time to go nowhere. Time was too short. They let you play for it and take a 20 minute break where when you get back on the bandstand you feel like working. But 15 minutes, it takes you almost five minutes to get back to the dressing room. Because this one stopped you, that one stopped you, you know, and talking about different things. First thing you know it's almost time to get back up on the bandstand.
